D006-D005_h001.question:
I’ve been like this for around eight months now. It started with me seeing people that aren’t really there. I’ll be on the night shift at the station and I’ll see a guy standing by pump 3 staring at me, but when I look again, no one’s there. Sometimes I see faces in the glass doors of the fridges, like they’re watching me. I also feel like the security cameras, the radio songs, even customers’ little comments are “about” me, like they’re sending me messages or judging me.

My thoughts and speech get weird. Words just start linking in my head because they rhyme, and I’ll say stuff like “gas, glass, class, pass” and kind of lose track of what I was actually trying to say.  

For a couple of weeks here and there during these months, I’ll suddenly get this rush of energy at work—trying to clean, restock, talk to customers all at once, jumping from one thing to another and not finishing anything. My mood flips fast, from feeling pumped and upbeat to snapping at people. But those bursts are short; most of the time I just feel flat and empty.  

For about three months now, nothing feels enjoyable at all. Even on days off, I just lie there, feeling like there’s no point. Sometimes when I’m near the road at the station, I get this urge to just step out into traffic—not with a plan, more like an impulse that scares me. I’ve messed up shifts, had complaints from customers, and I’m barely hanging on to the job.
D006-D005_h001.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Binge-Eating Disorder

D006-D005_h002.question:

I’ve also become convinced, at times, that everything is going to end soon—that the university, the city, maybe the whole world is about to be wiped out. It feels less like a fear and more like a fact.

My speech sometimes falls apart when I’m talking, especially under stress. In seminars I’ll start a sentence and then it turns into this jumble of words that even I can’t track. My husband says I “stop making sense.”

There was a stretch, maybe a few weeks within this, when I was unusually up and restless—pacing, unable to sit still, jumping from task to task, unable to concentrate on a single paper or email. But that passed, and the odd sensations and beliefs have just kept going.

More recently, for about three months, I’ve felt completely drained and stopped caring about my work. I canceled classes, ignored student emails, and stockpiled some of my anxiety meds planning to overdose. My husband found them and brought me here.

A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    B. Schizophrenia
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Binge-Eating Disorder

I know that sounds odd, but I can’t shake the feeling that he was seeing another woman; I read all kinds of things into old receipts and photographs.  

Around the same time, I started feeling like something was crawling on my arms and legs, like bugs under the skin, especially at night, but there’s nothing there when I look. When I try to explain this, I tend to go off on stories from the hospital or about my children and lose track of what you actually asked me.  

I used to enjoy gardening and church groups, but now I don’t get much pleasure out of anything. I feel mostly hollow, like there’s nothing inside. My appetite’s dropped off, and I wake up several times a night and just stare at the ceiling. Even talking feels slow and effortful; it takes me a while to get words out.  

There was a stretch, maybe a couple of weeks early on, when I felt strangely upbeat and full of energy—hardly sleeping, starting big cleaning projects—but that passed quickly and hasn’t come back.

The main thing that’s been going on, for around nine months now, is that I’m convinced I’m meant to be a world‑famous chef, like chosen for something bigger. My wife says I’ve started talking “around” things. She’ll ask a simple question like how my day was, and I drift off into talking about knives, or a sauce, and never really answer. At work I barely talk at all unless someone forces me to; it’s like the words just don’t come.
